# **Lane T1: Pre-Eruption Thera (Santorini) Land, Sea, and Climate Reference for Procedural 3D Reconstruction**

This technical reference supplies code-ready dimensions, landforms, sea-level offsets, climate parameters, and open starter datasets for reconstructing Late Bronze Age Thera (Late Cycladic I / Late Minoan IA) in the final months before the Minoan eruption (project window c. 1800–1500 BCE)1. Every Bronze Age date is indexed to both the **High (radiocarbon, IntCal20)** chronology (\~1609–1560 BCE; Egyptian Second Intermediate Period) and the **Low (Egyptian-linked)** chronology (\~1530–1500 BCE; early 18th Dynasty / New Kingdom) so future Mediterranean regions align cleanly2. Key builder caveats are stated directly: no directly dated Bronze Age sea-level index point exists on Santorini itself, Akrotiri's harbour remains unexcavated, exact pre-eruption northern lagoon depth and ring-land width could not be verified, and Linear A is undeciphered so no contemporary native island or town name is known1.

## **1\. Summary**

* **Set the scene in post-earthquake recovery during late spring or early summer:** One or more major earthquakes (estimated \~M 7\) struck Akrotiri months to a few years before the eruption, leaving active wall demolition, stone-sorting, and repairs underway when the eruption began in early-to-mid-summer (June or early July, shortly after the May pulse harvest) (Claims 7–9)2.  
* **Do not use modern Santorini's crescent coastline or deep southern caldera:** Immediately before the eruption, only the northern half of today's caldera held a shallow brackish-to-marine lagoon (inherited from the \~22 ka Cape Riva eruption), while a continuous southern rim joined Thera, Aspronisi, and southern Therasia, enclosing \~9.1–17.1 km³ of landmass later destroyed in the collapse (Claims 11, 12, 15, 18–20)1.  
* **Place Pre-Kameni inside the northern lagoon, and delete Palea and Nea Kameni:** Remove both modern Kameni islands (whose subaerial emergence began in 197/196 BCE) and insert the low-dome, dark black glassy andesite island of Pre-Kameni (reconstructed volume 2.2–2.5 km³, full range 1.6–3.0 km³) inside the northern caldera bay (Claims 13, 14, 32\)3.  
* **Keep a terrain toggle for the pre-eruption caldera sea entrance:** High-resolution bathymetry indicates the modern 3 × 1 km NW strait was carved post-eruption and the two SW straits slumped after flooding, leaving either a narrow/low northern outlet (dominant recent view) or a SW opening near Aspronisi (competing view) (Claims 15–17)1.  
* **Retain the metamorphic spine and older volcanic cores, but detach Monolithos:** Profitis Ilias (567 m a.s.l.), Mesa Vouno, Gavrilos, Athinios phyllite/schist cliffs, Peristeria/Megalo Vouno (≥528 ka), Skaros, the Akrotiri Peninsula core (650–580 ka), and Therasia's basement existed much as today, whereas eastern Monolithos was a separate offshore islet prior to LBA coastal progradation (Claims 23–26)9.  
* **Strip off up to 55–60 m of white Minoan tephra and undo \~3,600 years of coastal cliff retreat:** Subtract the post-eruption tuff mantle (locally \~40 m at Athinios and Vlychada, 0.3–5.5 m Phase 1 fall, 17–25 m fill in Mavrorachidi valley) and remove the deep post-eruption torrent ravine bisecting Akrotiri, noting that wave erosion has since cut soft outer cliffs back up to 1,181 m at Vlychada (Claims 27–31, 40, 43\)7.  
* **Lower sea level by \~3.0–3.7 m as the regional default (with a tunable slider):** Although Santorini lacks a directly dated LC I shoreline marker and exhibits active volcanic vertical motion (+60 to \+70 mm/yr unrest uplift; −6 to −30 mm/yr subsidence), neighboring Cycladic islands record Bronze Age sea level at −3.60 to −3.70 m below present MSL (Claims 33–36)17.  
* **Sit Akrotiri (\~20 ha) on a south-facing coastal headland with an indented shore:** Model the town along an elongated north–south ridge (+18.53 to \+19.86 m a.s.l. at Complex Delta, steeper eastern slope) overlooking shallow 20–40 m anchorage waters, placing the primary harbour candidate in the buried Mavrorachidi bay to the west (105–165 m inland of today's shore) or directly south behind a buried 30 m SE Cape Riva cliff (Claims 37–41)7.  
* **Populate the wider island with active LC I outposts and one ruined hilltop town:** Include active LC I sites at Raos, Chalarovounia, Balos, Potamos, Archangelos, Favatas, Ftellos, Mavromatis, and southern Therasia (Alaphouzos), but render Panaghia Koimisis on SE Therasia as abandoned Middle Cycladic ruins overgrown with olive shrubs (Claims 47–49)28.  
* **Do not add perennial rivers or urban rainwater cisterns:** Akrotiri lacks excavated Bronze Age cisterns (using roof waterspouts and stone street drains instead), coastal wells were likely brackish, and Santorini's only perennial natural spring today is the limestone cave spring of Zoodochos Pigi; rivers in West House frescoes are unattested physically on Thera (Claims 42, 45, 46\)19.  
* **Render a greener, slightly moister Mediterranean climate with clear summer skies and northerly Etesian winds:** Akrotiri wood charcoal indicates open oak woodland, pine, and cultivated olive groves on thin dark volcanic soil (not today's treeless pumice landscape), driven by October–April rains, nearly cloudless summers (\~0.3 oktas July–August), nocturnal-to-morning sea fog (*anedossa*), and dominant N/NW–NNE summer winds (Claims 44, 50–59)19.  
* **Bootstrap the heightfield from Copernicus GLO-30 \+ EMODnet DTM 2024 / GEBCO\_2026:** Combine free 30 m global Copernicus GLO-30 onshore elevation (note non-commercial and redistribution restrictions on raw/altered tiles; independent Value Added Products permitted) with CC BY 4.0 EMODnet (\~115 m) or Public Domain GEBCO\_2026 (\~500 m nominal) bathymetry, using CC BY 4.0 reconstructions (Nomikou et al. 2016; Karátson et al. 2018; Karstens et al. 2023\) as morphing blueprints (Claims 60–66)1.

## **4\. Assumptions checked**

* **T1-1:** **Partly confirmed** (Claims 11, 12, 15–17, 20\) — An older (\~22 ka) shallow brackish-to-marine lagoonal caldera occupied the *northern* half of modern Santorini, but the southern/western basins had not yet collapsed and the exact location and width of any pre-eruption sea opening (narrow northern outlet vs. SW opening vs. temporarily sealed) remain debated3.  
* **T1-2:** **Confirmed** (Claims 13, 14\) — A central volcanic island ("Pre-Kameni"), built of dark black glassy andesite starting at 20.2 ± 1.0 ka with a reconstructed volume of 2.2–2.5 km³ (full range 1.6–3.0 km³), stood inside the northern caldera bay3.  
* **T1-3:** **Partly confirmed** (Claims 15, 23, 24, 26–31, 40, 43\) — Profitis Ilias (567 m), Mesa Vouno, and the 650–580 ka volcanic core of Akrotiri already existed, but the southern caldera rim across Aspronisi later collapsed, Phase 4 fans extended outer coasts and attached Monolithos islet, waves later eroded up to 1,181 m at Vlychada (15.77 km² on Thera), 17–25 m of ash/gravel filled bays near Akrotiri, and a post-eruption ravine bisected the town3.  
* **T1-4:** **Contradicted (local Santorini marker could not be verified)** (Claims 33–36) — No directly dated LC I sea-level index point exists on Santorini itself, but neighboring Cycladic data place Bronze Age relative sea level noticeably lower at −3.70 ± 0.20 m (Mykonos–Delos–Rheneia) and −3.60 ± 0.30 m (Kea), Santorini paleocoastline modeling uses \~−3 m, and active volcanic vertical motion (+60 to \+70 mm/yr unrest uplift; −6 to −30 mm/yr subsidence) adds local uncertainty17.  
* **T1-5:** **Partly confirmed** (Claims 37–42) — Akrotiri was a major maritime town on a south-coast promontory overlooking shallow (20–40 m) anchorage waters, but no harbour installations have been excavated yet; boreholes point to a likely buried anchorage in Mavrorachidi valley to the west, while other specialists favor an embayment directly south of the site or twin east–west harbours7.  
* **T1-6:** **Confirmed** (Claims 50–59) — Stratified Akrotiri wood charcoal indicates a relatively moister, cooler Mediterranean environment supporting open oak woodland, pine, and olive cultivation alongside winter-sown cereals/pulses, although regional Aegean speleothems and marine cores show a gradual post-4.2 ka drying trend punctuated by a rapid Peloponnesian dry spell around 1600–1450 BCE36.  
* **T1-7:** **Partly confirmed** (Claims 22, 32\) — Neither Palea Kameni nor Nea Kameni existed before the LC I eruption and the first *subaerial* island emergence recorded historically was Hiera in 197/196 BCE, but IODP Expedition 398 cores and seismic data show *submarine* construction of Kameni Volcano inside the caldera began shortly after the \~1600 BCE collapse12.

## **5\. Debates**

### **1\. Absolute date of the Minoan eruption (High vs. Low Chronology)**

Radiocarbon-based **High Chronology** models place the eruption in Egypt's Second Intermediate Period, contemporary with Hyksos Avaris and Middle Bronze Age Canaan. IntCal20 Bayesian modeling of Akrotiri VDL and wider southern Aegean sequences yields \~1609–1560 BCE (95.4%; 1606–1589 BCE at 68.3%) (Manning 20222), reinforced by direct uncalibrated ¹⁴C measurements showing Akrotiri seeds (3344 ± 8 BP), Thera olive outer rings (3331 ± 10 BP), and Palaikastro tsunami bones (3351 ± 17 BP) are consistently older than pure straw from a Pharaoh Ahmose mudbrick (3230 ± 60 BP) (Bruins & van der Plicht 20254).  
Within the radiocarbon evidence itself, a mid-16th century shift remains debated. IntCal20 recalibration of the Thera olive yields 1621–1598 BCE (23.2%) or 1593–1540 BCE (72.3%), and a newly dated carbonized olive shrub from Panaghia Koimisis on Therasia dates slightly younger, increasing mid-16th century BCE probability (Pearson et al. 202333). Manning (202475), however, argues that this wider calendar spread stems from the ca. 1620–1540 BCE calibration curve plateau and opportunistic growth-band plasticity in olive wood.  
By contrast, **Low (Egyptian-linked)** archaeological synchronisms—based primarily on the first appearance of Cypriot White Slip I pottery and Theran pumice in early 18th Dynasty strata at Tell el-Daba—place the eruption after \~1540 BCE, often near \~1525 BCE (Driessen 2019 citing Warren, Wiener, and Höflmayer5). Höflmayer (201276) cautions that both Tell el-Daba pumice and secondary-context White Slip I sherds supply only a *terminus ante quem* rather than exact eruption timing.  
![][image3]

### **2\. Pre-eruption caldera geometry and sea openings**

The dominant recent consensus places the pre-eruption caldera solely in the northern basin, bordered by a continuous southern rim linking Thera, Aspronisi, and Therasia. Cosmogenic ³⁶Cl cliff exposure dating (Athanassas et al. 201611), bathymetry of the flood-carved NW strait and fresh SW landslide headwalls (Nomikou et al. 201612), lithic clast budgets (Karátson et al. 2018, 20203), and seismic collapse modeling (Karstens et al. 20231) support a shallow northern lagoon with either a narrow/low pre-existing northern outlet or a closed rim prior to post-eruptive flooding.  
A competing school places the pre-eruption sea opening in the southwest between Cape Akrotiri and Aspronisi, pointing to Minoan eruption deposits dipping inward toward the caldera in that sector (Friedrich et al. 198846; Friedrich 201314; Druitt & Francaviglia 19923). Similarly, Kordatzaki et al. (2018 citing Vougioukalakis 201556) reconstruct a habitable southern Therasia plain bordering a deep southern caldera entrance. An even earlier model by Heiken & McCoy (19843) placed the pre-existing caldera in the *southern* half and a central volcano in the north, but subsequent stratigraphy (Druitt et al. 1989/19993) and ³⁶Cl dating11 showed that southern Caldera 1 (172 ka) had long been filled in before the Late Bronze Age.

### **3\. Location and layout of Akrotiri's Bronze Age harbour**

Geoarchaeological boreholes drilled 105 and 165 m north of the modern beach in the \>200 m wide Mavrorachidi valley (west of Akrotiri) encountered \~3 m of rounded black-to-reddish volcanic sand beneath 17 m of ash and torrential gravel, favoring a buried prehistoric anchorage there while ruling out narrow valleys at the Akrotiri torrent mouth (\<50 m) and Mesovouna bay (\<150 m) (Bassiakos et al. 20237). Earlier seismic refraction also ruled out Potamos valley (\~500 m NE, floor above sea level) but revealed a buried 30 m high Cape Riva cliff southeast of Akrotiri that may have sheltered a bay immediately south of the town (Theodorakopoulou et al. 201826).  
Architecturally, Palyvou (2005, reviewed by Shaw 200634) compares Akrotiri's north–south promontory to contemporary Ayia Irini on Kea, suggesting twin east and west harbours. A separate iconographic hypothesis by Højen Sørensen et al. (201335) identifies the West House Ship Fresco's "Right Harbour" as a double harbour inside the caldera at Balos (north of Akrotiri) and the "Left Harbour" at Mouzaki Bay, whereas other scholars locate the "Arrival Town" on Akrotiri's south coast79 or view the frieze as a composite maritime scene rather than a literal map.

### **4\. Local relative sea level at Santorini c. 1650 BCE**

Regional beachrock and submerged archaeological stands across the northern and central Cyclades—Mykonos–Delos–Rheneia at −3.70 ± 0.20 m (1972–130 BCE23) and Ayia Irini on Kea at −3.60 ± 0.30 m (4000–2180 yr BP22)—indicate Bronze Age sea level lay substantially more than 1–2 m below present MSL, broadly consistent with Lambeck & Purcell's 0.7–0.93 mm/yr Aegean glacio-hydro-isostatic rise53 and Oikonomidis et al.'s (201618) \~−3 m contour on Santorini.  
However, transferring central-Cycladic subsidence directly to Santorini carries large uncertainty. Unlike the aseismically subsiding metamorphic Cycladic core23, Santorini sits on an active volcanic rift where Quaternary volcanotectonic uplift raised Akrotiri marine sediments \~100 m9 and modern geodetic monitoring records episodic caldera uplift up to \+60 to \+70 mm/yr alongside −6 to −30 mm/yr subsidence17. Without a directly dated LC I shoreline marker on Santorini itself, local Bronze Age sea level cannot be constrained to decimetre precision.

### **5\. Pre-eruption moisture and drying trajectory**

On-site Akrotiri wood charcoal indicates a relatively moister, cooler local environment supporting open oak woodland, pine, and long-term olive cultivation (Asouti 200336), and Palyvou (200534) raises the possibility that Akrotiri's lack of cisterns alongside stone street drainage reflects heavier rainfall than today.  
Regional Aegean palaeoclimate archives introduce nuance: Hermes Cave (Kluge et al. 202063), SE Aegean marine core NS-14 (Triantaphyllou et al. 201364), and the 2024 Aegean hydroclimate synthesis (Jacobson et al. 202465) document gradual long-term drying after the 4.2 ka event (even though consecutive regional aridity only peaks after \~3350 BP / \~1400 BCE). Moreover, Mavri Trypa Cave in the SW Peloponnese records a rapid dry excursion between 3550 and 3400 yr BP (\~1600–1450 BCE) inside an otherwise wetter baseline (Finné et al. 201762), while northern Greek speleothems diverge from Peloponnesian trends80, underscoring regional spatial variability.

## **6\. Game hooks**

*The items below are strictly design and engineering suggestions for your procedural 3D world, kept separate from the sourced evidence above.*

* **Uncertainty parameter sliders (builder / scholarly view mode):** Expose live procedural toggles for the three most consequential open debates—(1) Caldera Sea Entrance (Narrow North Outlet default / SW Opening near Aspronisi / Closed Lagoon), (2) Bronze Age Sea Level (−3.7 m Cycladic default / −3.0 m GIS / −1.5 m low-offset test), and (3) Chronology Mode (High: \~1600 BCE, Hyksos SIP vs. Low: \~1525 BCE, Early 18th Dynasty)—so future Mediterranean ports stay synchronized.  
* **Atmospheric *anedossa* morning fog and Meltemi wind shaders:** Generate a nocturnal-to-dawn marine mist layer (*anedossa*) drifting across terraced volcanic hillsides before clearing into bright summer skies (\~0.3 oktas) as dry northerly Etesian/Meltemi winds (Beaufort 4–6) build choppy whitecaps toward Crete.  
* **Post-earthquake Akrotiri world state:** Because an \~M 7 earthquake damaged Akrotiri months before the eruption, populate the streets with authentic repair details—stacked recyclable volcanic building stones, temporary timber shoring, household beds moved into open squares, and partially dismantled unstable walls—while omitting the post-eruption torrent ravine.  
* **Navigational landmarks and island visibility:** Contrast the low, dark glassy lava dome of Pre-Kameni (with faint hydrothermal venting) inside a shallow turquoise-green northern lagoon bordered by pale stromatolite shoals against the warm volcanic headland of Akrotiri and the detached offshore islet of Monolithos on the eastern sailing approach.  
* **Contrasting rural outposts and abandoned ruins:** Connect bustling coastal Akrotiri by trail and boat to terraced elite buildings at Raos overlooking the lagoon, pastoral Ftellos, and the southern Therasia settlement at Alaphouzos—contrasted with the quiet, abandoned Middle Cycladic hilltop ruins of Panaghia Koimisis overgrown with olive shrubs on SE Therasia.  
* **Hydrological realism without anachronistic rivers:** Omit urban rainwater cisterns in favor of roof waterspouts and stone street drains, make coastal lowland wells brackish, and place a limestone cave spring on Profitis Ilias/Mesa Vouno (modeled by analogy with Zoodochos Pigi, explicitly tagged Grade B/C) rather than perennial rivers.
